title: Live Earthquake Statistics
summary_easy: A live browser dashboard on the US Geological Survey earthquake feed. It computes how much rarer big quakes are than small ones and how fast aftershocks fade, and it keeps a log of every correction USGS makes to its own catalog while the page is open. On October 8, 2026, California's b-value came out at 0.73 with a bootstrap range of 0.66 to 0.85.
summary_deep: The page loads the USGS all_week GeoJSON feed once and polls all_hour every 60 s and all_day every 5 minutes, merging every response into one catalog keyed by preferred id, with an alias map over every associated id and the updated timestamp as the version clock. Deletions are inferred conservatively from the day feed only, with a newer response guard and a 10 minute aging margin. Per region it estimates the magnitude of completeness by maximum curvature plus 0.2, the Aki-Utsu maximum likelihood b-value with a Shi and Bolt error, and a 200 resample bootstrap that recomputes Mc each time. Aftershocks are selected with Gardner-Knopoff windows and fitted to Omori-Utsu by Ogata's maximum likelihood on a grid with a profile likelihood range for p, refusing below 30 aftershocks; hourly counts are tested against a Poisson rate from the median of the previous 24 hours. A first failing test led to a calibration study: 93.7% bootstrap coverage over 300 synthetic catalogs.

sheet.easy:
## What it is
- A live page on the US Geological Survey earthquake feed, computed entirely in the browser, with no server.
- Two jobs at once: the classic statistics of seismology on the past week, and a log of every correction USGS makes while the page is open.

## The data
- Three GeoJSON feeds, regenerated by USGS every minute: past week (loaded once, about 1.4 MB, about 2,000 events), past hour (every 60 s), past day (every 5 min).
- Oct 8, 2026: 1,949 events, 1,905 earthquakes. Explosions, quarry blasts and ice quakes are left out of every statistic.

## The questions and methods
| Question | Method |
| --- | --- |
| How much rarer is each bigger quake? | Gutenberg-Richter b-value, Aki maximum likelihood with Utsu's correction |
| Smallest size fully recorded? | Maximum curvature plus 0.2 (Woessner and Wiemer 2005) |
| How sure are we? | Shi and Bolt error plus a 200 resample bootstrap that recomputes completeness |
| How fast do aftershocks fade? | Gardner-Knopoff windows, Omori-Utsu fit (30 aftershocks needed) |
| Which hours were unusual? | Poisson test against the median of the previous 24 hours, flag below 0.001 |
| What did USGS change? | Merge by id and updated time; log revisions, id changes, deletions |

## Results (Oct 8, 2026)
- California b = 0.727 +- 0.033, bootstrap 0.661 to 0.851, Mc 0.9. Alaska 0.717, 0.609 to 0.843.
- All events pooled: 0.34, a sign of mixed magnitude scales, and the page says so.
- No aftershock fit live (best sequence had 12 aftershocks). Injected synthetic 200 aftershocks: p = 1.08 vs true 1.1.
- 45 minutes of polling: 9 new events, 7 revisions, 0 deletions, 6 magnitude changes averaging 0.19.

## The testing story
- First b-value test failed: interval missed b = 1 on one seed.
- 300 synthetic catalogs: 93.7% coverage. Now a test needs 16 of 20 catalogs to cover.
- 29 tests on node, nothing to install, CI on node 22 and 24.

## Honest limits
- Mixed magnitude scales; one week is short; no live deletion seen; no declustering; revision log lost on reload; coarse coastlines.
sheet.deep:
## Architecture
- `quakes/seismo.js`: pure functions, no DOM, no d3. Merge, completeness, b-value, bootstrap, Gardner-Knopoff, Omori-Utsu, Poisson rule, `analyze()`.
- `quakes/app.js`: `loadWeek()` once (retry after $\min(120, 5 \cdot 2^{a})$ s), then `ui.poll` all_hour every 60 s and all_day every 300 s. Analysis memoised per (catalog version, region, minute).
- `assets/ui.js`: `poll()` with 20 s AbortController timeout, in flight guard, backoff $\min(\text{every} \cdot 2^{\min(f-1,4)}, 600\,\text{s})$; first poll always runs, later ones skip while hidden; `visibilitychange` triggers a poll. Paint scheduler on one requestAnimationFrame loop; ingestion never pauses.
- Map: d3-geo 3.1.1, Equal Earth, topojson-client 3.1.0, world-atlas 2.0.2 land 1:110m, PB2002 plates (Bird 2003). Depth colour log scale 0 to 700 km; ripples every 4 s for last hour events.
- Links from the feed pass `safeHref` with an https allowlist of earthquake.usgs.gov.

## Feed fields used
`id`, `properties.ids` (",a,b,"), `mag`, `magType`, `place`, `time`, `updated`, `status` (automatic, reviewed, deleted), `type`, `net`, `url`, `felt`, `tsunami`, `sig`, `geometry.coordinates = [lon, lat, depth]`, `metadata.generated`.

## Merge rules
- `events` Map(primary id), `alias` Map(any id to primary), `gone` Map(deleted), `prev[key]` = previous response end and ids, `log` (cap 5,000), `touches` (cap 20,000), `version`.
- Accept a version only if `e.updated > cur.updated`. Drop events older than 7 days.
- `diffEvent`: mag tol 0.005, depth tol 0.05 km, epicenter move >= 0.5 km (haversine, R = 6,371 km), magType, status, place, type. No field changed means a touch.
- Preferred id change: resolved through `ids`, logged as one revision with `prevId`.
- Deletion by absence: day feed only (keyed window), only if `win.end > prev.end`, only if event time $\ge$ end $-$ span $+$ 10 min, missing under every id. Deletion by `status = deleted`. Restore only with newer `updated` or a response generated after the deletion. `gone` expires after 2 weeks.

## Completeness and b-value
- Bins: `binIndex(m) = round(round(100 m) / 10)`, $\Delta M = 0.1$.
- $M_c = \text{MAXC} + 0.2$, MAXC = mode bin (ties to smaller). Needs 50 events; b needs 50 at or above $M_c$.
$$\log_{10} N(\ge M) = a - bM$$
$$\hat b = \frac{\log_{10} e}{\bar M - (M_c - \Delta M/2)}$$
$$\sigma_b = 2.30\, b^2 \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i (M_i - \bar M)^2}{n(n-1)}} \approx \frac{b}{\sqrt n}, \qquad a = \log_{10} N(\ge M_c) + b M_c$$
- Bootstrap: 200 resamples of the regional catalog with replacement, recompute $M_c$ then $b$, drop resamples with fewer than 50 above $M_c$, percentile 2.5 to 97.5 with linear interpolation, mulberry32 seeded.

## Aftershocks
- Gardner-Knopoff: $d = 10^{0.1238M + 0.983}$ km; $t = 10^{0.032M + 2.7389}$ d for $M \ge 6.5$, else $10^{0.5409M - 0.547}$ d. M 5: about 40 km, 143.7 d. M 4: 41 d.
- Candidates $M \ge 4$; a later larger event inside the window marks a foreshock; most aftershocks wins.
- Omori-Utsu $n(t) = K/(t+c)^p$, Ogata (1983) likelihood:
$$\log L = n \log K - p \sum_i \log(t_i + c) - K\, I(c,p), \quad I(c,p) = \frac{(T+c)^{1-p} - c^{1-p}}{1-p}, \quad I = \ln\frac{T+c}{c} \text{ at } p=1$$
$$\hat K = n / I(c,p) \Rightarrow \log L(c,p) = n \log(n/I) - pS(c) - n$$
- Grid: c 61 log spaced values 0.001 to 1 d; p 0.40 to 2.00 step 0.02 (81). Cost $O(61n + 61 \cdot 81)$. Profile range $\{p : 2(\ell_{max} - \ell_p(p)) \le 3.841\}$. Edge flags. Needs 30 aftershocks. Rate plot: 4 log bins per decade.
- No catalog wide declustering: windows only select one sequence.

## Busy hours
- 168 UTC hourly bins; for hour $i \ge 24$, $\lambda = $ median of previous 24, else mean if median is 0, floor $1/24$. Flag if $P(X \ge k) < 0.001$, $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$. 144 hours tested.

## Test strategy
- Recover known parameters from data drawn from the model: b = 1 at n = 5,000; MAXC within 0.1 under a Gaussian taper; p = 1.1, c = 0.05 at n = 1,000.
- Check formulas exactly: Shi and Bolt to 1e-12, $K I = n$ to 1e-6, Omori integral continuous at p = 1.
- Check calibration across seeds: 16 of 20 bootstrap intervals cover b = 1; profile ranges cover p.
- Every merge rule: revision, deletion, restoration, aging out, stale response, preferred id, older version, touch, status deleted.

## Limitations
- Mixed magnitude scales; one week; constant Mc per region; no declustering; Poisson on clustered counts; deletions never seen live; log not persisted; Gardner-Knopoff calibrated on Southern California; coarse coastlines.

narration.script: An earthquake catalog keeps changing after the fact. Automatic solutions get reviewed, magnitudes move, events merge under a new id, and some are deleted. So I built a page that does two jobs: it computes seismology statistics on the past week of USGS data, and it logs every change the catalog makes while you watch. The data is three GeoJSON feeds. I load the week once, then poll the past hour every minute and the past day every five minutes. Every response is merged into one catalog keyed by id, with an alias map for the other networks' ids, and the updated timestamp decides which version wins. On that catalog I find the magnitude of completeness by maximum curvature plus 0.2, fit the b-value by Aki's maximum likelihood with Utsu's binning correction, and bootstrap it 200 times, recomputing completeness each time. For aftershocks I take Gardner-Knopoff windows around the busiest mainshock and fit Omori-Utsu by maximum likelihood once there are 30 aftershocks. On October 8, California gave b = 0.73 with a range of 0.66 to 0.85, and Alaska 0.72. Pooled across everything it was 0.34, which reflects mixed magnitude scales, and the page says so. In 45 minutes of polling it recorded 9 new events and 7 revisions, with six magnitudes moving by 0.19 on average. What broke: my first b-value test failed because a 95% interval missed the truth on one seed. I checked coverage over 300 synthetic catalogs, got 93.7%, and now test coverage across 20 catalogs. No sequence reached 30 aftershocks that week, so there was no live Omori fit. Next, I would persist the revision log for weeks and split b by magnitude type.

narration.prompt: Give me the full technical story.
narration.script: The starting observation is that a live earthquake feed is a mutable table. USGS publishes an automatic solution within minutes, then replaces it with reviewed or better solutions, sometimes from another network under another id. A statistic computed from the feed inherits all of that, so I treat the revision log as an output with the same standing as the b-value. Ingestion first. The page loads all_week once, about 1.4 MB, then polls all_hour every 60 seconds and all_day every five minutes. USGS regenerates them every minute, so faster polling gains nothing. Every response goes through one merge function. Events are keyed by preferred id, and an alias map covers every id the feed lists for that event. The updated timestamp is the version clock: anything equal or older is dropped, because the three feeds are cached separately and an old copy can arrive late. When the preferred id changes, the new record still lists the old id, so it resolves to the same event and is logged as one revision. That happened live: an Alaska network solution became the national one, moving the depth from 20.9 to 35 km. Deletions are the subtle part, because a deleted event can just disappear. I infer a deletion only from the day feed, only when the new response was generated after the previous one, and only for events at least 10 minutes inside the 24 hour window, so aging out is never mistaken for deletion. A deleted event comes back only with a newer version or in a newer response. No deletion happened in 55 minutes, so that path is tested only on synthetic feeds. Then the statistics. Completeness is maximum curvature, the most populated 0.1 bin, plus 0.2 from Woessner and Wiemer, because maximum curvature runs low. The b-value is Aki's maximum likelihood estimate, log10 e over the mean magnitude minus Mc minus half a bin; the half bin is Utsu's correction for rounded magnitudes. Shi and Bolt gives a standard error, but it assumes Mc is known, so I also bootstrap the whole pipeline 200 times with a fixed seed, recomputing Mc on every resample. Results from October 8: California 0.727 plus or minus 0.033, bootstrap 0.661 to 0.851, above Mc 0.9; Alaska 0.717. Global M4.5 and up gave 1.5 from only 62 events, and 39 resamples were dropped for falling under 50 events, which the page reports. Pooled everything gave 0.34, which is a mixture of ml, mb, md and mww from different networks, and the page says that beside the number. For aftershocks, every M 4 or larger event is a candidate, Gardner-Knopoff windows collect later events, and a candidate followed by something bigger is a foreshock. With 30 or more aftershocks I fit Omori-Utsu by Ogata's maximum likelihood with K profiled out, on a grid of 61 c values and 81 p values, and report the 95% profile likelihood range for p. That week the best candidate had 12 aftershocks, so there was no live fit; an injected synthetic sequence of 200 came back at p = 1.08 against a true 1.1. Testing is where the project earned its keep. My first b test failed: the interval missed b = 1 on one seed. Over 300 catalogs coverage was 93.7%, with a spread of 0.0183 against a mean Shi and Bolt error of 0.0176, so it was an ordinary miss. I changed the seed and added a test that requires 16 of 20 catalogs to cover. For p, the spread is 0.21 at 120 aftershocks, so that test checks interval coverage instead of a point tolerance. Limits: mixed magnitude scales, one week, no declustering, and a revision log that lives in browser memory.

narration.prompt: Explain it to someone without a technical background.
narration.script: The US Geological Survey publishes every earthquake it detects, and the list keeps changing. A quake first appears with a computer's estimate, then a scientist checks it, and its size or location can change. My page reads that list every minute and does two things. It works out the patterns scientists expect, like how much rarer a big quake is than a small one, and how quickly aftershocks fade after a large quake. And it keeps a diary of every correction the survey makes while you watch. In one 45 minute session it caught seven corrections. I also tested that the math gives the right answer on made up data where I already knew the answer, and when one test failed, I found out why instead of loosening it.

narration.prompt: How do you decide where the b-value fit starts?
narration.script: The fit starts at the magnitude of completeness, the size above which the catalog records essentially everything. I estimate it by maximum curvature, which is the 0.1 bin with the most events, and add 0.2 because maximum curvature is known to run low; that correction is from Woessner and Wiemer. I need 50 events to attempt it and 50 above it to fit. I chose it over goodness of fit or stability methods because the bootstrap reestimates it 200 times per refresh in a browser. The test builds a catalog with a smooth detection roll off below 2.0 and requires maximum curvature within 0.1.

narration.prompt: How do you detect deletions without false positives?
narration.script: A deleted event usually just disappears, so I infer deletions from absence, with three guards. I only compare consecutive past day responses, never the hour feed, because events leave the hour feed constantly by aging. I only compare when the new response was generated after the previous one, because the feeds are cached and an older copy can arrive late. And I skip anything within 10 minutes of the window edge, since it may simply have aged out. An event also has to be missing under every id it ever had. If it reappears in a newer response, it is restored and logged. None happened live in 55 minutes, so this is tested on synthetic feeds.

narration.prompt: How do you know the bootstrap interval is right?
narration.script: I can't know from one catalog, so I measured coverage. I generated 300 synthetic catalogs of 5,000 events with a true b of 1 and ran the full pipeline, including the completeness estimate, on each. The interval contained 1 in 93.7% of them. The estimates averaged 0.9965 with a spread of 0.0183, while Shi and Bolt averaged 0.0176, so the analytic error is slightly small. With 300 catalogs, 93.7% is about one standard error below 95%. The suite now requires at least 16 of 20 catalogs to cover, which a calibrated procedure fails well under one percent of the time.

narration.prompt: What would you need to fit aftershocks on live data?
narration.script: A week with a sizeable mainshock in a well instrumented region. The fit needs 30 aftershocks, and the best candidate that week was an M 5.5 in Alaska with 12. When a sequence does arrive, two things matter. Completeness is much worse in the first hours because small events hide in the mainshock's waves, which inflates c, so I would add a time varying completeness level or a higher magnitude cut. And Gardner-Knopoff windows collect background events too, so I would compare against a declustered background. I would also extend the window past one week, because a seven day catalog truncates the sequence.

narration.prompt: A pooled b of 0.34 is nonsense. Why is it on the page?
narration.script: I agree it is nonsense as a physical estimate, and the page says that right beside it. Pooling mixes California's tiny local magnitudes with worldwide events measured on body wave and moment scales, and each network has a different completeness level, so the slope flattens. Its small standard error of 0.013 shows how a precise number can still be wrong when the model does not fit. I left it visible with the magnitude type mix, ml 51%, mb 29%, md 15% and mww 4%, because a reader who sees the bad number explained learns why the regional numbers are the ones to trust.

narration.prompt: This is a toy: two thousand events in a browser.
narration.script: The volume is small, and I would not claim otherwise. The hard parts are correctness under revision and calibrated statistics, and those do not get easier with volume. The merge handles version ordering across separately cached feeds, preferred id changes, aging out and stale responses, each with a test. The statistics are implemented from the papers and checked for coverage over hundreds of synthetic catalogs. At a hundred times the data I would move to the FDSN service with updatedafter, an append only version table and offline bootstraps, and the logic would carry over unchanged.

cards.q: What is Live Earthquake Statistics, in one sentence, and what does it do technically?
cards.easy: A browser page that pulls the past week of earthquakes from the US Geological Survey, refreshes it every minute, computes the textbook statistics of seismology on it, and keeps a log of every correction USGS makes to its own catalog while the page is open.
cards.deep: Everything runs client side in JavaScript with no server. quakes/app.js loads all_week.geojson once, then polls all_hour.geojson every 60 s and all_day.geojson every 5 minutes. Every response goes through mergeCatalog in quakes/seismo.js, which keys events by id, resolves alternative ids through an alias map, compares updated timestamps, and logs revisions and deletions. On the merged catalog, analyze() computes per region: the magnitude of completeness by maximum curvature plus 0.2, the Aki-Utsu maximum likelihood b-value with a Shi and Bolt error and a 200 resample bootstrap that recomputes Mc each time, a Gardner-Knopoff window around the busiest mainshock with an Omori-Utsu maximum likelihood fit once it has 30 aftershocks, and a Poisson test on hourly counts. seismo.js has no DOM, so the node:test suite imports the same file the page runs. The premise is that statistics on a live feed inherit the feed's revisions, so the two are shown together.

It computes the classic seismology statistics, the b-value and the aftershock decay, and it logs every revision USGS makes while you watch. cards.q: Why is revision tracking part of a statistics dashboard at all?
cards.easy: USGS posts automatic solutions within minutes, then reviewed or better solutions replace them: magnitudes move, depths change, events merge under a new id, and a few are deleted. Every number computed from the feed moves with them, so the page shows the statistics and the corrections side by side.
cards.deep: An automatic solution is computed by software from the first arriving waves. A reviewed one replaces it later, sometimes from a different network, for example the Alaska network's aka solution replaced by the national us solution. In the 45 minute log, 6 magnitudes moved by 0.19 on average. For a b-value built on a few hundred events above Mc, a shift of a few tenths in the newest events changes which 0.1 bin they land in, and MAXC is the mode of that histogram, so Mc itself can move. The last hour and last day counts are the most provisional numbers on the page because automatic solutions dominate them. A visible revision log turns 'provisional' from a footnote into something the reader can watch happen.

cards.q: What is the polling schedule, how does it back off, and why that cadence?
cards.easy: Load the week once, then check the past hour every 60 seconds and the past day every 5 minutes. USGS regenerates the feeds once a minute, so polling faster gains nothing. The hour feed is tiny and catches new events quickly; the day feed is larger and is the one used to spot deletions.
cards.deep: loadWeek() fetches all_week once with cache: 'no-cache' and on failure retries after min(120 s, 5 s x 2^attempt). After the first merge it starts ui.poll on all_hour every 60e3 ms and all_day every 300e3 ms. poll() aborts a request after 20 s through an AbortController, skips a tick while one is in flight, and after a failure waits min(every x 2^min(fails - 1, 4), 10 min), so the hour feed backs off 60, 120, 240, 480, then 600 s. cards.q: Define ml, md, mb, mww and mwr, and say why the feed mixes them.
cards.easy: They are different ways to measure an earthquake's size. ml (local) uses peak shaking near the source, md (duration) uses how long the shaking lasts, mb (body wave) uses the first P waves at distant stations, and mww and mwr are moment magnitudes from the size of the fault slip. US regional networks report small local quakes in ml or md; worldwide coverage is mostly mb and mww at M 4 and up.
cards.deep: ml is the Richter style local magnitude from peak amplitude, calibrated in Southern California and unreliable far away and for large events. md is the duration magnitude from the length of the wave train, used by networks such as Northern California and Hawaii. mb is the teleseismic body wave magnitude from short period P waves in the first seconds, and it saturates for large events. Moment magnitude comes from the seismic moment (rigidity times fault area times slip); mww is the W phase moment magnitude USGS computes for larger global events and mwr a regional moment tensor. The scales agree only roughly, so one histogram that mixes them is not one Gutenberg-Richter population. Above Mc in the run: All events ml 51%, mb 29%, md 15%, mww 4%; California ml 52%, md 47%; Global M4.5+ mb 71%, mww 27%. magTypeMix() computes these shares on events at or above Mc and the page prints them beside b.

cards.q: State the Gutenberg-Richter law and explain what a and b mean.
cards.easy: The number of earthquakes at or above a given magnitude falls by a constant factor for every step up in magnitude. With b = 1, each whole unit up means ten times fewer quakes. a says how active a region is overall; b says how that activity splits between small and large events.
cards.deep: log10 N(>= M) = a - b M, where N is the cumulative count. Equivalently, magnitudes above the completeness level are exponentially distributed, f(M) = beta exp(-beta (M - Mc)) with beta = b ln 10. One magnitude unit changes the count by a factor of 10^b, so b = 0.73 means about 5.4 times fewer events per unit (10^0.73 is about 5.37). b near 1 is typical of tectonic regions; values run roughly 0.5 to 2, with high values in swarms and volcanic areas. A b far from 1 can also mean a flawed or mixed catalog. The law describes a complete catalog, so the fit starts at Mc. fmd() returns per 0.1 bin counts and the cumulative counts that the chart plots on a log axis, filling empty bins with zero. The page computes a = log10 N(>= Mc) + b Mc; for California, log10(370) + 0.727 x 0.9 gives the logged 3.22.

cards.q: What is the magnitude of completeness, and what is maximum curvature?
cards.easy: Small quakes are easy to miss, so below some size the catalog is missing events and the counts stop rising. The magnitude of completeness, Mc, is the smallest size above which essentially every event is recorded. Maximum curvature (MAXC) takes the most populated 0.1 magnitude bin as the estimate.
cards.deep: On a non cumulative frequency magnitude histogram, a complete catalog rises exponentially toward small magnitudes; detection loss makes it bend over and fall. MAXC picks the bin with the largest count, which is where the cumulative curve bends most sharply. It is fast and needs no fitting, but it underestimates Mc, most of all when the roll off is gradual, which is why Woessner and Wiemer (2005) recommend adding 0.2. Mc varies in space and time: the dense California networks reach Mc 0.9 here, Global M4.5+ sits at 4.8, and right after a large mainshock Mc rises for hours because small events are buried in the mainshock's coda.

cards.q: How is Mc computed in code, including ties and minimum sample size?
cards.easy: Each magnitude goes into a 0.1 bin, the bin with the most events wins (ties go to the smaller magnitude), and 0.2 is added. With fewer than 50 earthquakes the page refuses to estimate Mc and says how many it has.
cards.deep: completeness(mags) maps magnitudes to integer bins with binIndex, counts them in a Map, and maxcK returns the bin with the highest count, breaking ties toward the smaller k. Then kMc = k + round(0.2 x 10) and mc = kMc / 10. Working in integer tenths avoids comparisons like 1.2 >= 1.2000000000000002. Constants: DM = 0.1, MAXC_CORRECTION = 0.2, MIN_MC_EVENTS = 50, MIN_B_EVENTS = 50. A refusal returns { ok: false, n, need }, and gutenbergRichter separates 'few' (under 50 events in the region) from 'fewAbove' (Mc found, but under 50 events above it). The test 'MAXC finds a known Mc +- 0.1 under tapered incompleteness' draws 40,000 Gutenberg-Richter magnitudes from 0.5, keeps each one below Mc = 2.0 with probability exp(-((2.0 - m)/0.15)^2), and requires MAXC within 0.1 of 2.0 and the corrected Mc to equal MAXC + 0.2 exactly.

cards.q: Why maximum curvature plus 0.2 instead of a goodness of fit or b-value stability method?
cards.easy: It is simple, fast and well documented, and the page reruns it 200 times inside the bootstrap on every refresh, in a browser. The fixed 0.2 correction removes most of its known low bias. The cost is that it can still be off when the histogram bends gradually.
cards.deep: Alternatives: goodness of fit (Wiemer and Wyss 2000) picks the lowest Mc at which a Gutenberg-Richter model explains 90 or 95% of the observed distribution; MBS picks where b stops changing as the cutoff rises; EMR (Woessner and Wiemer 2005, after Ogata and Katsura 1993) fits Gutenberg-Richter above Mc and a cumulative normal detection curve below it. Each costs a fit per candidate cutoff, and the bootstrap reestimates Mc on every resample, so an O(n) mode is what fits the per refresh budget. MAXC's failure mode is a smeared roll off from mixed networks, where the mode sits below the true Mc even after the correction; including incomplete bins flattens the slope and pushes b down. The tradeoff is written in the method text, and the tapered incompleteness test checks MAXC lands within 0.1 on a smooth synthetic roll off.

cards.q: Derive the Aki maximum likelihood b-value and explain Utsu's binning correction.
cards.easy: Above Mc, magnitudes behave like an exponential distribution, and the best estimate of an exponential rate is one over the average excess above the threshold. So b is log10(e) divided by how far the mean magnitude sits above the threshold. Because magnitudes are rounded to 0.1, the threshold is moved down half a bin.
cards.deep: With f(M) = beta exp(-beta (M - M0)) for M >= M0, the log likelihood of n events is n ln beta - beta sum (M_i - M0). Setting the derivative to zero gives beta_hat = 1 / (mean(M) - M0), so b = beta / ln 10 = log10(e) / (mean(M) - M0) (Aki 1965). Catalog magnitudes are rounded to bins of width dM, so an event labelled Mc came from [Mc - dM/2, Mc + dM/2); Utsu's correction sets M0 = Mc - dM/2. Without it, mean(M) - Mc understates the true mean excess and b comes out biased high. In code, akiUtsuK sums bin indices k >= kMc, takes mean = s / n / 10 and denom = mean - (mc - DM/2), returns b = Math.LOG10E / denom, and refuses when n < 2 or denom <= 0. The estimator assumes one exponential population, independent events, a sharp complete threshold and no upper magnitude limit; mixed scales, clustering and a wrong Mc each break one of those.

cards.q: What is the Shi and Bolt uncertainty, and why is it close to b over root n?
cards.easy: It is a standard error for b computed from the spread of the magnitudes: 2.30 times b squared times the standard error of the mean magnitude. For an exponential distribution that works out to about b divided by the square root of the event count.
cards.deep: sigma_b = 2.30 b^2 sqrt( sum (M_i - mean)^2 / (n (n - 1)) ) (Shi and Bolt 1982), where 2.30 is ln 10. It is the delta method on b = log10(e) / (mean - M0): the derivative of b with respect to the mean is -b^2 ln 10, multiplied by the standard error of the mean. For an exponential with rate beta = b ln 10, the standard deviation of M is 1/beta, so sigma_b is about 2.30 b^2 / (2.30 b sqrt(n)) = b / sqrt(n), which is Aki's original error. Shi and Bolt uses the observed spread, which behaves better when the sample departs from a pure exponential. The test recomputes it by hand on 4,000 synthetic events to 1e-12 and checks it is within 0.01 of b / sqrt(n). Its blind spot is that Mc is treated as known, which is why the page also bootstraps.

cards.q: Why does binIndex round twice, and what bug does that prevent?
cards.easy: Values like 1.4999999999999998 come out of floating point arithmetic. Rounding first to hundredths and then to tenths puts them in the bin a person would expect, so a single event cannot flip bins and move Mc.
cards.deep:
```js
export function binIndex(m) { return Math.round(Math.round(m * 100) / 10); }
```
The inner round removes noise below 0.005 and the outer round gives the 0.1 bin as an integer. cards.q: What are Omori's law and the modified Omori (Omori-Utsu) law? What do K, c and p mean?
cards.easy: After a big quake, the aftershock rate falls off roughly like one over the time since the mainshock. The modified law lets the decay be steeper or gentler (p) and keeps the rate finite at time zero (c). K sets how productive the sequence is.
cards.deep: Omori (1894): n(t) = K / (t + c). Utsu (1961): n(t) = K / (t + c)^p. K scales with productivity and with the lower magnitude cut; c is a short time offset in days that keeps the rate finite at t = 0 and also absorbs early incompleteness; p is the decay exponent, typically 0.7 to 1.5. With p > 1 the total number of aftershocks over infinite time is finite; with p <= 1 the integral diverges. The model is a non stationary Poisson process: given the rate, aftershock times are independent, and aftershocks of aftershocks are folded into one rate. ETAS (epidemic type aftershock sequence) models make every event a potential parent instead.

cards.q: Write down the Omori-Utsu likelihood used in the fit and show how K is profiled out.
cards.easy: Treat aftershock times as a Poisson process whose rate decays like K over (t + c)^p. The likelihood rewards a rate that is high where events happened and penalises the total number the rate predicts. For any c and p, the best K is the observed count divided by the integral of the decay, so only c and p need searching.

Setting d/dK = n/K - I = 0 gives K = n / I. Substituting, K I = n and log L(c, p) = n log(n / I) - p S(c) - n with S(c) = sum log(t_i + c). omoriIntegral switches to the log form when |p - 1| < 1e-9; one test checks continuity at p = 1 +- 1e-6 to within 1e-4, and another checks K x I = n to within 1e-6.

cards.q: What is a profile likelihood interval, and why is 3.841 the cutoff?
cards.easy: For each candidate p, take the best fit over the other unknowns, then keep every p whose best fit is not much worse than the overall best. 'Not much worse' is set by a chi-square rule so the range covers the truth about 95% of the time.
cards.deep: Profile log likelihood: l_p(p) = max over (K, c) of log L(K, c, p). By Wilks' theorem, 2 (l_max - l_p(p_true)) is asymptotically chi-square with one degree of freedom, whose 95% quantile is 3.841, so {p : 2 (l_max - l_p(p)) <= 3.841} is an approximate 95% interval. The code filters pGrid with that rule and returns the min and max. Unlike a Wald interval (estimate +- 1.96 SE) it can be asymmetric and follows the shape of the likelihood. It is asymptotic, so coverage can drift at small n: simulation gave 95% at 120 aftershocks and 93% at 1,000 over 200 sequences each, within Monte Carlo noise of 95% (about 1.5 points at 200 sequences). It is only as fine as the 0.02 grid and is cut short if it reaches the grid edge.

If a bigger quake follows inside the window, the candidate was a foreshock and is skipped. The candidate with the most aftershocks is the one plotted.

M 5 gives about 40 km and 143.7 days; M 5.5 gives 46.1 km and 267.9 days; even M 4 gives 41 days, longer than the one week catalog, so in practice every later event within d counts. findSequence sorts by time and, for each candidate, scans forward while time <= tEnd, keeping events within d by haversine; a later event larger than the candidate marks it a foreshock. Ties on aftershock count go to the larger mainshock. Cost is O(C n) for C candidates (151 for All events in the run). The windows were calibrated on Southern California, so elsewhere they are a convention. Terms: a mainshock is the largest event of a sequence, foreshocks precede it, aftershocks follow it.

cards.q: Does the code decluster the catalog? Where does that matter?

cards.deep: Declustering removes dependent events (foreshocks and aftershocks) to leave a background catalog closer to Poisson; common methods are Gardner-Knopoff windows applied across the whole catalog, Reasenberg's cluster linking, and stochastic declustering from an ETAS fit. cards.q: How is the aftershock rate plotted, and how does early incompleteness affect the fit?
cards.easy: Aftershock times are counted in time bins that grow by a fixed factor, four per factor of ten, and each count is divided by the bin width to give events per day. On log axes an Omori decay is close to a straight line with slope minus p. Right after a big quake many small aftershocks are missed, which flattens the earliest part, and the fit absorbs that into c.
cards.deep: logBinnedRate(times, T, perDecade = 4) starts at 10^(floor(4 log10 t_min) / 4), uses edges lo x 10^(i/4) capped at T, and returns each bin's geometric midpoint sqrt(a b), count k and rate k / (b - a). Empty bins come back with rate 0 because a log axis cannot draw them, and the table view lists them. The test checks that counts sum to the number of positive times and rate x width equals k. Early incompleteness: in the first minutes to hours, the mainshock coda and overlapping waveforms hide small events, so Mc is temporarily higher than the weekly value. The fit uses all magnitudes in the window, so the deficit appears as a larger c, which mixes physics with detection. A cleaner fit would use a time varying Mc or a high magnitude cut, at the cost of fewer events.

cards.q: How does the page decide that an hour was unusually busy?
cards.easy: For each hour, it takes the median count of the 24 hours before it as the expected rate, then asks how likely the observed count, or more, would be by chance under a Poisson model. If that chance is below 1 in 1,000, the hour is flagged.

The tail P(X >= k) = 1 - sum_{j<k} e^-lambda lambda^j / j! is computed by poissonSf in log space to avoid overflow, and the hour is flagged if it is below 0.001. A median keeps a burst from inflating its own baseline in the hours after it. The floor of one event a day stops quiet regions from flagging any single event: at lambda = 1/24, P(X >= 1) is about 0.041 and is not flagged, while P(X >= 2) is about 0.00084 and is, which a test checks. The first 24 hours lack a full baseline, so 144 of 168 hours are tested.

cards.q: What is statistically fragile about the busy hour test?
cards.easy: Earthquakes cluster, so a Poisson model is the wrong model for raw counts, and the test will flag most aftershock sequences. It also runs 144 tests per region, so a few chance flags are expected over many weeks. The page treats a flag as a sign of clustering and never as a forecast.
cards.deep: (1) Overdispersion: clustered counts have variance well above their mean, so Poisson tail probabilities come out too small and flags come easily; the median baseline offsets only part of that. (2) Multiple testing: 144 hourly tests at 0.001 give an expected 0.144 false flags per region per week even if counts truly were Poisson, so one flag in a week is unremarkable; a Bonferroni level would be 0.001/144, about 7e-6. (3) The 24 hour trailing baseline adapts to a slow ramp, so gradual increases are never flagged, and daily cycles in detection (more cultural noise in daytime hides small events) can create a daily rhythm in counts. (4) The current partial hour is tested as it stands, so early in an hour it is less likely to flag. A negative binomial baseline or a declustered rate would be the principled fixes.

cards.q: Describe the catalog data structure and the basic merge rule.
cards.easy: One map from event id to the latest version of each event, plus a second map from every alternative id to the main one. A new response replaces an event only if its updated time is newer. Every change that matters goes into a log.

cards.q: What counts as a revision versus a touch, and what tolerances are used?

cards.q: How does the merge handle an event whose preferred id changes?
cards.easy: The feed lists every id that belongs to an event. When the national solution replaces the Alaska network's, the record arrives under a new id but still lists the old one, so the page knows it is the same quake and logs one revision, 'id A to B'.

If that primary differs from e.id, rekey is true: the old record is unindexed, the new one is indexed under all its ids, and the log entry carries prevId. Without this, the old id would vanish from the next day response and be logged as a deletion while the new id showed up as a new event, inflating both counts and double counting the quake in between. cards.q: How are deletions detected, and what guards stop false deletions?
cards.easy: A deleted event can simply vanish from the summary feed. So the page compares each past day response with the previous one: an event that disappeared under all of its ids, while it should still be inside the 24 hour window, is logged as deleted. It comes back, with a log entry, if a later response has it again.
cards.deep: Two paths: a feature with status 'deleted' (logged via 'status') and absence (via 'absent'). Absence checks run only for keyed windows, which means the day feed, and only when the new response's end (metadata.generated) is later than the previous one. For each id in the previous response: skip if present now under any id; skip if its time is before end - span + DELETE_MARGIN (10 minutes), since it may just have aged out; otherwise unindex it and move it to gone. Restoration: a gone id returns only if its updated is newer or the response was generated after the deletion was recorded, so a stale cache cannot resurrect it but a feed glitch cannot hide it for good. gone entries expire after two weeks. Tests cover revision plus deletion, restoration, aging out, stale responses, and status deletions.

cards.q: Why does only the past day feed drive deletions, and why the rule against comparing an older response?
cards.easy: The hour feed is too short: events leave it every minute just by getting older, and everything in it is also in the day feed. And the three feeds are cached separately, so an older copy can arrive after a newer one; comparing against it would make recent events look deleted.
cards.deep: ingest() passes { key: 'day', span: DAY, end: g } for the day feed and { span: HOUR, end: g } with no key for the hour feed, and mergeCatalog runs absence checks only for keyed windows. On a one hour window, the 10 minute aging margin would cover a sixth of the window, and a true deletion is caught within five minutes on the day poll anyway. The stale response rule (win.end > prev.end) exists because a cache can serve a response generated at 19:08 after one generated at 19:13; without the rule, events added in between would be logged as deleted and then restored, producing pairs of fake log entries. The test 'a response older than the previous one is never compared for deletions' checks that state.prev.day.end keeps the newer end.

cards.q: Your first b-value test failed. What happened, and what did you change?
cards.easy: Its synthetic catalog had a true b of 1, and the 95% interval came out 1.015 to 1.070, missing it. That is expected sometimes, since a 95% interval should miss about one time in twenty. So the single catalog test got a different seed, and a new test checks coverage across 20 catalogs.
cards.deep: The tempting fix was to widen the interval or loosen the tolerance until the test passed. The real question was whether the procedure is calibrated, and one catalog cannot answer that. tests/sim/quakes_b_coverage.mjs ran 300 catalogs of 5,000 events with true b = 1: coverage 93.7%, mean b 0.9965, spread 0.0183 against a mean Shi and Bolt error of 0.0176, mean interval width 0.0676. So the original failure was an ordinary miss; the test file notes that seed 7, for example, lands outside its interval at 2.4 sigma. The suite now has two tests: one seeded catalog that must recover b within 0.05 with an interval that covers 1 and is narrower than 0.2, and one that needs at least 16 of 20 catalogs to cover. Changing the seed is only honest because the coverage test now carries the statistical claim.
cards.say: My first b-value test failed, and it failed for the right reason. A 95% interval misses about one time in twenty, and I had an unlucky seed. Over 300 synthetic catalogs it covered 93.7% of the time, so I changed that test's seed and added one that needs 16 of 20 catalogs to cover.

cards.q: Quote the b-value calibration numbers and what each one checks.
cards.easy: Over 300 synthetic catalogs with true b = 1: the average estimate was 0.9965, estimates varied by 0.0183, the Shi and Bolt error averaged 0.0176, and the bootstrap interval contained 1 in 93.7% of catalogs. 99.7% of estimates were within 0.05 of 1.
cards.deep: Mean 0.9965 checks bias: with MAXC + 0.2 and Utsu's correction the estimator is close to unbiased. sd 0.0183 against mean sigma 0.0176 shows Shi and Bolt is about right but slightly small, consistent with ignoring Mc uncertainty. Coverage 0.937 checks the bootstrap. Mean width 0.0676 compares with 2 x 1.96 x 0.0183 = 0.0717 for an interval matching the observed spread, so the bootstrap runs about 6% narrow, which fits the coverage shortfall. within005 = 0.997 is the share with |b - 1| < 0.05. Caveat: the synthetic catalogs are exactly exponential, with every event at or above 1.0 and 0.1 rounding (MAXC then puts Mc at 1.2), so they test the code and the estimator under its own assumptions and say nothing about real catalog quirks.

cards.q: A 95% interval with 93.7% coverage: is that a bug?
cards.easy: Probably a small real shortfall and not a bug. With 300 catalogs the coverage estimate has its own uncertainty of about 1.3 points, so 93.7% is about one standard error below 95%. Percentile bootstrap intervals are known to run slightly narrow.
cards.deep: Monte Carlo SE of coverage at N = 300 is sqrt(0.95 x 0.05 / 300) = 0.0126, so 0.937 is about 1 SE low and not significant alone. The width comparison (0.0676 against the 0.0717 implied by the observed spread) points the same way. Plausible causes: percentile intervals ignore bias and skew (b is the reciprocal of a mean excess, so its distribution is right skewed), and resampling a binned catalog full of ties understates the variability of the MAXC mode. Fixes: BCa intervals, more resamples (200 leaves only 5 values beyond each 2.5% quantile, so the endpoints are noisy), or a parametric bootstrap from the fitted exponential. The 16 of 20 rule fails a truly calibrated 95% procedure with probability about 0.26%, and one at 93.7% about 0.7%; with fixed seeds the test is deterministic anyway.

cards.q: What does the test suite cover, and how does CI run it?
cards.easy: 29 tests on node's built in test runner with nothing to install: 27 for the seismology module and 2 for shared duration formatting. They recover known values from synthetic catalogs and check every merge rule. CI runs them on node 22 and 24 for every push and pull request.
cards.deep: tests/quakes.test.mjs covers binning; Gutenberg-Richter (Aki-Utsu recovery at n = 5,000, coverage in 16 of 20, the Shi and Bolt formula and 1/sqrt(n), MAXC under tapered incompleteness, refusals, fmd counts, bootstrap reproducibility); aftershocks (Gardner-Knopoff at M 5 and the 6.5 branch, haversine including the antimeridian, Omori recovery of p = 1.1 and c = 0.05 at n = 1,000 with K x I = n, integral continuity at p = 1, log bins conserving counts, findSequence skipping foreshocks); merging (revision plus deletion, restoration, aging out, stale responses, preferred id, same or older versions and the seven day bound, touches, status deletions); bursts (spike, mean and floor fallbacks, UTC hour binning); regions; and one end to end analyze() on a synthetic California sequence of 120 aftershocks. The workflow has no install step on purpose, which proves the analytic modules have no third party dependencies. The portfolio card's figure of 27 tests counts the seismology file alone.

cards.q: Show how the tests generate synthetic Gutenberg-Richter catalogs and Omori-Utsu aftershock times.
cards.easy: Both use inverse transform sampling: draw a uniform random number and push it through the inverse of the distribution's cumulative function. Magnitudes come out exponential and are then rounded to 0.1; aftershock times come out with the Omori-Utsu decay over a fixed window.

cards.q: How is the page structured so the statistics can be tested without a browser?
cards.easy: All the math and merging lives in one file with no page code, quakes/seismo.js. The page imports it to draw the map and charts, and the test suite imports the same file in node. The map libraries load from a CDN, but every number is still computed if they fail.
cards.deep: Layout: index.html; quakes/seismo.js (merging, completeness, b-value, bootstrap, windows, Omori, the Poisson rule; no DOM and no d3); quakes/app.js (polling, map, ripples, charts); assets/ (util.js with rng, quantile, poissonSf and ols; ui.js with poll, feed badges, the paint scheduler and safeHref; charts.js). The analysis is memoised per (catalog version, region, minute) so every painter shares one result. The map uses d3-geo 3.1.1 with an Equal Earth projection (an equal area world projection), topojson-client 3.1.0 to decode Natural Earth 1:110 million land from world-atlas 2.0.2, and PB2002 plate boundaries (Bird 2003) pinned to a commit. Dots are coloured by depth on a log scale from 0 to 700 km and fade to 25% over the week, with ripples every 4 s for last hour events. ES modules do not load from file://, so it is served with python3 -m http.server.

cards.q: What are the honest limitations of the project?
cards.easy: Pooled b-values mix magnitude scales and are not physical. One week is too short for most aftershock fits. No deletion was ever seen live. Coastlines are coarse for Hawaii and Puerto Rico. And every recent number is provisional because automatic solutions change.
cards.deep: (1) Mixed ml, md, mb and mww, even within one region. (2) One week: regional b from a few hundred events carries wide intervals and a single sequence can dominate. (3) No live deletion in 55 minutes of polling, so the absence logic is tested only on synthetic feeds. (4) MAXC + 0.2 is the simplest Mc method, and Mc is assumed constant across the week and the region, though it rises after large events and varies with network density inside a box. (5) Gardner-Knopoff windows were calibrated on Southern California, and regions are latitude and longitude rectangles. (6) No declustering, and a Poisson test on clustered counts. (7) The revision log lives in browser memory, is lost on reload, and is capped at 5,000 entries. (8) 1:110 million coastlines.
evidence: portfolio: None occurred in 55 minutes of polling, so the deletion logic has only been exercised on synthetic feeds.

cards.q: What breaks at 10x and 100x scale, and what would production need?
cards.easy: At ten times the data, a month of events, the browser still copes but downloads and the bootstrap get slow. At a hundred times, years of catalog, it needs a server, a database, and statistics updated incrementally instead of recomputed from scratch every minute.
cards.deep: 10x: all_month is the natural step. The payload grows toward ten times the 1.4 MB week, the bootstrap is O(B N) per refresh (200 x 20,000 draws), and findSequence is O(C n) with more candidates; all still feasible, but worth moving to a Web Worker so painting stays smooth. One Mc per region starts to fail because completeness varies inside a box. 100x: summary feeds stop being the right source. Use the ComCat FDSN event service with updatedafter to pull only changed events and includedeleted to see deletions explicitly rather than inferring them from absence; store versions in an append only table keyed by (event id, updated) so revision history survives reloads; compute Mc and b on spatial grids with per cell sample size rules; run bootstraps offline on a schedule; serve precomputed aggregates. FDSN caps a query at 20,000 events, so backfills must page by time.

cards.q: What would you do next?
cards.easy: Keep a long revision log to measure how much and how fast magnitudes change by network. Split b-values by magnitude type. Decluster the catalog before the busy hour test. And compare better completeness methods.
cards.deep: (1) Persist revisions server side for weeks and report revision counts and mean |dM| by network, magnitude and age, which turns the 45 minute anecdote into a measurement. (2) b by magType within a region (California ml against md) to show the scale effect directly. (3) Decluster with Gardner-Knopoff across the catalog or Reasenberg, then test hourly rates on the background with a negative binomial alternative. (4) Compare MAXC + 0.2 with goodness of fit and MBS on the same catalogs, and use BCa intervals or more resamples. (5) A time varying Mc after mainshocks in the Omori fit, or an ETAS model to separate background from triggered events. (6) Exercise the deletion path on real recorded deletions through the FDSN includedeleted option.

cards.q: Why build this in browser JavaScript instead of Python with ObsPy, or a proper backend?
cards.easy: Because the goal was a live public page with no server to run, and the math is small enough to write and test directly. The cost is reimplementing estimators that mature libraries already have, which is why each one is tested against known values.
cards.deep: Concede: Python's seismology stack has tested implementations, and a backend would persist the revision log, which today vanishes on reload. Defend: the workload is one small GET a minute and about 2,000 events, so a static page on GitHub Pages costs nothing to run and anyone can open it; the same seismo.js runs in the page and in node, so tests cover exactly the shipped code; CI proves there are no dependencies. The reimplementation risk is handled by recovering known parameters from synthetic catalogs and checking calibration over 300 catalogs, which is stronger evidence than trusting a library call. Persistence is the real gap, and it is the first item on the next steps list.
cards.say: Fair point: ObsPy and a backend would give me tested code and persistence. I wanted a page anyone can open with nothing running behind it, and the data is two thousand events. I paid for that by writing the estimators myself, so I tested them against synthetic truth, including coverage over 300 catalogs.

cards.q: California b = 0.73 is far from 1. Isn't your estimator broken?
cards.easy: The estimator recovers b = 1 on synthetic catalogs, averaging 0.9965 over 300 of them, so the code is not the first suspect. The low value describes this catalog: one week of data, ml and md mixed, and possibly an Mc still a little low.
cards.deep: Concede: 0.73 is low for California, and the interval [0.661, 0.851] excludes 1. Defend: the code path is validated on known truth, so the remaining candidates are the data. Above Mc, California is ml 52% and md 47%, two scales from different networks with different calibrations; MAXC + 0.2 can still sit low on a gradual roll off, and including incomplete bins flattens the slope; and one week includes small swarms that are not declustered. The test of these explanations is cheap: split by magType and by network, and recompute b at Mc + 0.1 and + 0.2 to see whether it climbs. Until then the honest claim is 'the slope of this catalog above 0.9', and that is how the page states it.
cards.say: The estimator averages 0.9965 when the truth is 1, so I trust the code. What I don't trust is that a week of mixed ml and md magnitudes is one population. I report 0.73 as this catalog's slope above Mc 0.9, and I would test it by splitting by magnitude type.

cards.q: 200 bootstrap resamples is too few.
cards.easy: For a 95% percentile interval it is on the low side, since only 5 resamples lie beyond each end. It was chosen because the page reruns the bootstrap, with Mc recomputed on every resample, on each refresh in the browser. Simulation showed 93.7% coverage, close to nominal.
cards.deep: Concede: endpoint noise from 200 resamples is real, and the coverage of 93.7% with a width about 6% below the observed spread suggests a slightly narrow interval. Defend: the budget is 200 full pipeline fits (bin, mode, Aki-Utsu) on up to about 2,000 events per refresh on the main thread, the seed is fixed so the number does not jitter between refreshes, and the shortfall is measured rather than assumed. The fix is mechanical: move the bootstrap into a Web Worker or compute it once per catalog version, then raise B to 1,000 or 2,000 and consider BCa intervals.
cards.say: I agree 200 is the floor for a 95% percentile interval. It is the budget for recomputing Mc 200 times on every refresh in a browser. I checked what it costs: 93.7% coverage over 300 synthetic catalogs. If I moved the bootstrap off the main thread, I would go to 1,000 or 2,000.

cards.q: Your Poisson burst test is meaningless because earthquakes cluster.
cards.easy: As a hazard test it would be, and the page says a flag is not a forecast. What it does is mark hours where clustering is strong enough to beat a median baseline at 1 in 1,000, which is a useful pointer to a swarm or a sequence.
cards.deep: Concede: raw counts are overdispersed and the Poisson tail is too optimistic about rarity; 144 tests per region also mean occasional chance flags. Defend: the median baseline means a burst does not raise its own expectation, the mean fallback and 1/24 floor stop quiet regions from flagging single events, and the label is descriptive ('clustering, usually an aftershock sequence or a swarm'). The principled version would decluster first and use a negative binomial or ETAS based expectation, which is listed as next work.
cards.say: It would be meaningless as a hazard test, and the page says it is not a forecast. What it does is mark hours where clustering beats a median baseline at 1 in 1,000. That points you at a swarm or a sequence. The principled version would test a declustered rate with an overdispersed model.

cards.q: 45 minutes of polling is an anecdote. Why quote 7 revisions?
cards.easy: It is an anecdote, and the write up treats it as one. The number shows the merge logic working on real revisions, including a preferred id change that a naive merge would count as one deletion plus one new event.
cards.deep: Concede: one afternoon, small California and Alaska events, 7 revisions; no rate or bias can be estimated from it, and no deletion occurred. Defend: the claim attached to it is narrow, that the merge correctly classified every change it saw, with each change printed in runs/2026-10-08-quakes-poll.txt so a reader can audit it line by line. The measurement worth trusting needs days of logs per network and magnitude, and that is the first item on the next list.
cards.say: It is an anecdote, and I call it one. The number shows the merge working on real revisions, including a preferred id change that a naive merge would count as a deletion plus a new event. The measurement I would trust needs days of logs per network, and that is first on my list.

cards.q: You never fit Omori on live data, so the aftershock part is untested.
cards.easy: On live data, true: no sequence that week had 30 aftershocks, so the page drew points without a fit. The fit itself is tested on synthetic sequences, and its uncertainty interval was checked for coverage.
cards.deep: Concede: real sequences have early incompleteness, secondary aftershocks and background events inside the window, none of which synthetic data has. Defend: the estimator recovers p = 1.1 and c = 0.05 from 1,000 synthetic times, K x I = n is checked to 1e-6, the profile range covered the true p in 95% of 200 sequences at 120 aftershocks and 93% at 1,000, and an injected 200 aftershock sequence went through the live ingest path and returned p = 1.08. Refusing below 30 events is a deliberate choice, since simulation shows p would be loose to about 0.4. A week with a real M 6 is the missing test.
cards.say: On live data, yes: no sequence that week had 30 aftershocks, so the page drew points without a fit. The fit is tested, though. It recovers p = 1.1 from synthetic times, and its range covered the true p in 95% of 200 simulated sequences at 120 aftershocks. A real mainshock week is the missing test.

cards.q: Explain this project to a hiring manager in under a minute.
cards.easy: A live earthquake dashboard that computes real seismology statistics in the browser and keeps an audit trail of every correction the source makes.
cards.deep: Lead with the problem (a mutable public feed), then the two outputs (statistics and revision log), one result, and the testing discipline.
cards.say: I built a live dashboard on the USGS earthquake feed that runs entirely in the browser. It computes the standard seismology statistics and logs every correction USGS makes to its own catalog while the page is open. California came out at b = 0.73 with a bootstrap range, and in 45 minutes it caught 7 revisions. Every estimator is tested against synthetic data with a known answer, including whether its intervals cover the truth.
evidence: portfolio: Polling for 45 minutes from 19:19 UTC recorded 9 new events and 7 revisions.

cards.q: Explain the merge and deletion logic to a staff engineer.
cards.easy: Events are versioned by their updated time, matched across ids through an alias map, and deletions are inferred conservatively from one feed only.
cards.deep: Cover the version clock, alias resolution for preferred id changes, keyed window absence checks with the aging margin and the stale response guard, and the restoration rule.
cards.say: Each event is keyed by its preferred id, with an alias map over every associated id, and the updated timestamp is the version clock, so older copies from separate caches are dropped. A preferred id change resolves through the alias map and becomes one revision. Deletions are inferred only from the day feed, only when the response is newer than the last one, and only for events at least 10 minutes inside the window. A deleted event comes back only with a newer version or a newer response.

cards.q: Explain to a product manager why the page shows a number with a warning instead of hiding it.
cards.easy: The pooled b-value of 0.34 is shown with a note because explaining a misleading number teaches the reader more than hiding it.
cards.deep: Use the pooled b as the example; explain who reads the page and what the warning does for trust.
cards.say: When you pool every network, the b-value comes out at 0.34, which looks precise and is physically meaningless. I could have hidden it, but someone will compute it anyway. So the page shows it next to a sentence saying it reflects mixed magnitude scales, and it lists the mix. People trust the regional numbers more because the page is open about the bad one.
evidence: portfolio: Across all events pooled together, b was 0.34.

cards.q: Explain to a recruiter what this project shows about you.
cards.easy: It shows statistics implemented from the original papers, checked for calibration, plus the data engineering a constantly changing public feed needs.
cards.deep: Keep it plain: live data, real statistics, careful testing, honest reporting.
cards.say: It shows I can take a messy live data source and get trustworthy numbers out of it. I implemented the statistics from the original seismology papers, tested that their error bars are right, and built the plumbing that tracks when the source changes its mind. I also report what did not work, like the week with no aftershock sequence big enough to fit.
